overview: Batch processing is a data processing approach where bounded chunks of data are collected over a period and processed together as a group, typically on a schedule or when a dataset reaches a certain size, rather than one event at a time.
It optimizes for high throughput and efficiency, accepting higher latency (minutes to hours) in exchange for the ability to process very large volumes of data cost-effectively.
Batch processing is implemented with engines like Apache Spark, Hadoop MapReduce, and scheduled SQL jobs, orchestrated by schedulers such as Apache Airflow or cron.
learningObjectives: Understand what batch processing is and the throughput-vs-latency trade-off it makes.
Learn the core concepts of batch jobs: bounded datasets, scheduling, windows, and idempotency.
Contrast batch processing with stream processing and know when to choose each — a classic interview comparison.
coreConcept.formalDefinition: Batch processing is the execution of data processing jobs over a finite, bounded dataset that has been accumulated over time, where the entire group of records is processed together in a single run. Jobs are typically triggered on a schedule or by data availability, optimize for throughput, and tolerate latency on the order of minutes to hours.
coreConcept.simpleExplanation: Batch processing is like doing all your laundry once a week instead of washing each sock the moment it gets dirty. You wait until you have a full load, then process everything together in one efficient run. It takes longer to get any single item clean, but you handle a huge amount at once with minimal effort.
coreConcept.historicalContext: Batch processing dates back to early mainframe computing in the 1950s and 60s, when jobs were submitted on punch cards and run in batches to maximize expensive machine utilization. It scaled massively with Google's MapReduce paper (2004) and Apache Hadoop (2006), which made distributed batch processing of petabyte-scale data on commodity hardware mainstream. Apache Spark later improved on MapReduce with in-memory processing, and batch remains the backbone of most analytics and data-warehouse pipelines.

whyItMatters.business: Batch processing powers the daily/weekly reports, dashboards, billing runs, and analytics that businesses rely on, turning large volumes of accumulated data into insight cost-effectively.
whyItMatters.engineering: Batch jobs are simpler to reason about than streaming — they operate on complete, bounded datasets, making logic, testing, reprocessing, and debugging more straightforward.
whyItMatters.scalability: Distributed batch engines (Spark, Hadoop) scale horizontally to process terabytes or petabytes by parallelizing work across many nodes.
whyItMatters.cost: Processing in large groups amortizes overhead and lets you run on cheaper, schedulable resources (off-peak windows, spot instances), making it far cheaper per record than always-on streaming.
whyItMatters.reliability: Because batch jobs run on bounded data and can be made idempotent, failed runs can be safely re-run from a known point, simplifying recovery.

coreComponents.name: Bounded Dataset (the batch)
coreComponents.definition: A finite, complete set of records accumulated over a time period or size threshold that the job processes together.
coreComponents.purpose: To define a clear, fixed input so the job has a definite start and end.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Represent a known chunk of data (e.g., one day's events) with clear boundaries for processing and reprocessing.
coreComponents.examples: All sales transactions from yesterday; a directory of files dropped during the last hour.

coreComponents.name: Batch Job
coreComponents.definition: The unit of work that reads the bounded dataset, applies processing logic, and writes output, running to completion and then terminating.
coreComponents.purpose: To transform or aggregate the entire batch in a single, finite execution.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Read input, apply transformations/aggregations, handle failures/retries, and produce a deterministic output for the batch.
coreComponents.examples: A nightly Spark job aggregating daily revenue; a scheduled SQL job rebuilding a summary table.

coreComponents.name: Scheduler / Orchestrator
coreComponents.definition: The system that triggers batch jobs on a schedule or when dependencies/data are ready, and manages their order and retries.
coreComponents.purpose: To run jobs at the right time, in the right order, with dependency and failure management.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Trigger jobs (cron/schedule/sensor), enforce DAG dependencies, retry failures, and alert on SLA breaches.
coreComponents.examples: Apache Airflow DAGs, cron jobs, AWS Glue/EMR scheduled jobs, dbt Cloud schedules.

internalWorking: A scheduler triggers the job at a defined time or when a data-availability sensor confirms the batch is complete.
The engine reads the bounded input dataset (often partitioned by date), splitting it into parallel tasks distributed across worker nodes.
Each task processes its partition (map/filter/join/aggregate); intermediate results are combined (shuffle/reduce) to produce the final output.
The job writes results to the target (warehouse table, files, partitions), records success/state, and terminates; the scheduler then triggers any downstream dependent jobs.
coreConcept.architectureFlow: Accumulated Data (bounded batch) -> Scheduler triggers Job -> Distributed Engine reads partitions -> Transform/Aggregate (parallel tasks) -> Write Output -> Trigger downstream jobs
dataFlowWalkthrough: 1. Throughout the day, order events are written to a date-partitioned landing location (e.g., s3://events/dt=2026-06-17/).
2. At 1 AM, Airflow's sensor confirms yesterday's partition is complete and triggers the nightly Spark job.
3. Spark reads the full day's partition, splits it across executors, joins to dimensions, and aggregates to daily totals in parallel.
4. The job writes the daily-summary partition atomically and idempotently (overwriting that partition), marks success, and Airflow triggers the downstream reporting job.

keyTerminology.meaning: The property that re-running a batch job for the same input produces the same result without duplicating or corrupting data.
keyTerminology.importance: Essential for safe retries and reprocessing; usually achieved by overwriting a partition keyed on the batch window.

keyTerminology.meaning: The time or size boundary that defines a batch, commonly a date partition such as one day's data.
keyTerminology.importance: Defines the unit of processing and reprocessing and enables partition pruning and atomic overwrites.

keyTerminology.meaning: Re-running batch jobs for historical windows to populate or correct past data.
keyTerminology.importance: A core operational task that idempotent, partition-based batch design makes safe and simple.

importantConcepts.explanation: Batch maximizes throughput (records processed per unit time) by amortizing overhead over large groups, at the cost of latency — results are delayed until the batch runs.
Batch operates on bounded (finite, complete) datasets, which is what makes its logic, reprocessing, and correctness simpler than streaming over unbounded data.

variationsAndTypes: **Scheduled batch:** Jobs run at fixed times (hourly, nightly) — the most common form.
**Triggered/event-driven batch:** A job starts when a dataset arrives or a sensor confirms data is ready.
**Micro-batch:** Very small, frequent batches (seconds to minutes) used to approximate near-real-time processing (e.g., Spark Structured Streaming micro-batches).
advantages: **High throughput:** Efficiently processes very large volumes by amortizing overhead across the whole batch.
**Cost-effective:** Runs on schedulable, cheaper resources (off-peak, spot) and avoids always-on infrastructure.
**Simpler logic and reprocessing:** Bounded data makes jobs easier to write, test, debug, and backfill.
**Mature tooling:** Well-supported engines (Spark, Hadoop) and orchestrators (Airflow) with strong ecosystems.
disadvantages: **High latency:** Results are delayed until the next scheduled run — not suitable for real-time needs.
**Resource spikes:** Large jobs can cause bursty resource demand during the processing window.
**Stale data between runs:** Downstream consumers see data only as fresh as the last batch.
**Reprocessing whole windows:** Correcting data often means re-running an entire partition rather than a single record.

tradeOffs.whenToUse: Use batch processing when latency of minutes to hours is acceptable, when you process large volumes periodically (daily reports, billing, ETL/ELT loads, ML feature generation, backfills), and when cost-efficiency and simplicity matter more than real-time freshness.
tradeOffs.whenToAvoid: Avoid batch when you need low-latency, per-event reactions — fraud detection, real-time alerting, live dashboards, or recommendation updates — where stream processing is the right fit.

coreConcept.realWorldAnalogy: Batch processing is like a mail sorting facility that collects letters all day and sorts the entire pile overnight in one efficient operation, rather than dispatching a courier for every single letter the instant it arrives. Sorting in bulk is far more efficient per letter, but any individual letter waits until the nightly sort.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Batch processing is outdated and stream processing has replaced it.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Batch remains the backbone of most analytics, reporting, and data-warehouse pipelines. Batch and stream are complementary; many systems use both (e.g., Lambda/Kappa architectures), choosing each per use case.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Batch always means slow, once-a-day jobs.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Batch frequency ranges from daily to micro-batches every few seconds. 'Batch' refers to processing bounded groups, not to a specific schedule.

productionConsiderations.scalability: Scale horizontally by partitioning input (typically by date) and adding workers/executors. Watch for data skew, which makes a few tasks dominate runtime; mitigate with salting or repartitioning.
productionConsiderations.reliability: Make jobs idempotent (overwrite the target partition keyed on the batch window) so failed runs can be safely re-run, and use a scheduler with dependency-aware retries.
productionConsiderations.faultTolerance: Distributed engines like Spark recompute lost partitions on node failure; checkpoint long pipelines and persist input so a failed job restarts without re-ingesting source data.
productionConsiderations.monitoring: Track job duration, input/output row counts, SLA adherence (did the job finish before consumers need it), data-quality checks, and resource utilization to catch slowdowns and skew.
productionConsiderations.security: Secure data at rest and in transit, control access to input/output stores, and mask sensitive fields in outputs; run jobs with least-privilege service accounts.
productionConsiderations.costOptimization: Schedule jobs in off-peak windows, use spot/preemptible instances with retries, right-size clusters, and process incrementally (only new partitions) rather than full reloads.
productionConsiderations.performance: Partition and prune inputs, use columnar formats (Parquet/ORC), tune parallelism to avoid skew, and prefer set-based/vectorized operations over row-by-row processing.

codeExamples.title: A Nightly PySpark Batch Job (Idempotent Partition Overwrite)
codeExamples.overview: This Spark batch job processes one bounded day of order events into a daily-summary table, writing idempotently by overwriting only that date's partition.
codeExamples.code:
import sys
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

run_date = sys.argv[1]  # e.g. '2026-06-17', passed by the scheduler

spark = (SparkSession.builder
    .appName("daily_orders_batch")
    .config("spark.sql.sources.partitionOverwriteMode", "dynamic")
    .getOrCreate())

# Read ONLY the bounded batch: one day's partition
orders = (spark.read.parquet("s3://events/orders/")
    .filter(F.col("dt") == run_date))

# Aggregate the batch in parallel across the cluster
daily = (orders
    .filter(F.col("status") == "COMPLETED")
    .groupBy("dt", "region")
    .agg(F.sum("amount").alias("daily_revenue"),
         F.countDistinct("order_id").alias("order_count")))

# Idempotent write: overwrite ONLY this date's partition so reruns are safe
(daily.write
    .mode("overwrite")
    .partitionBy("dt")
    .parquet("s3://warehouse/daily_orders/"))

spark.stop()
codeExamples.breakdown: The job receives a run_date from the scheduler, reads only that day's bounded partition (not the full history), aggregates it in parallel, and writes back overwriting just that partition. Dynamic partition-overwrite mode plus filtering by run_date makes the job idempotent — re-running the same date produces the same result without duplicates.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: A `daily_orders` dataset partitioned by date, with one row per (dt, region) containing daily_revenue and order_count for the processed day.
codeExamples.commonIssues: Without dynamic partition-overwrite mode, `mode('overwrite')` can wipe the entire table instead of one partition. Reading the full path without filtering by dt scans all history. Skew on region can make a few tasks slow.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Always filter to the target partition for partition pruning, use Parquet/columnar formats, repartition or salt skewed keys, and size the cluster to the batch volume.

codeExamples.title: A Scheduled SQL Batch Job Orchestrated by Airflow
codeExamples.overview: This shows a parameterized SQL batch transformation and a minimal Airflow DAG that runs it nightly, waiting for the day's data to land first.
codeExamples.code:
-- daily_revenue.sql (parameterized by the scheduler's execution date)
DELETE FROM analytics.daily_revenue WHERE revenue_date = '{{ ds }}';

INSERT INTO analytics.daily_revenue (revenue_date, region, total_revenue, order_count)
SELECT '{{ ds }}'                AS revenue_date,
       region,
       SUM(amount)              AS total_revenue,
       COUNT(DISTINCT order_id) AS order_count
FROM raw.orders
WHERE order_date = '{{ ds }}'
  AND status = 'COMPLETED'
GROUP BY region;
codeExamples.breakdown: The DELETE-then-INSERT keyed on the execution date `{{ ds }}` makes the job idempotent: re-running a date first clears that day's rows, then re-inserts them, so reruns and backfills never duplicate data. The job processes a single bounded day (WHERE order_date = '{{ ds }}'). In Airflow, a sensor waits for the day's data, then a SQL operator runs this statement nightly with retries.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: The `analytics.daily_revenue` table contains exactly one set of rows per processed date; re-running a date replaces rather than duplicates that date's data.
codeExamples.commonIssues: Forgetting the DELETE makes reruns duplicate rows. Not waiting for data to land produces partial results. Hardcoding the date instead of using `{{ ds }}` breaks backfills.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Partition the target by date for fast delete/insert, use a data-availability sensor before running, and enable scheduler retries with backoff for transient failures.

endToEndExample.businessProblem: An e-commerce company needs a daily revenue-and-orders report by region, available every morning by 6 AM, computed from the previous day's high-volume transaction logs.
endToEndExample.inputData: Date-partitioned raw order events (order_id, region, amount, status, order_date) landing continuously in object storage throughout each day.
endToEndExample.architecture: Airflow orchestrates a nightly Spark batch job that reads the previous day's partition from S3, aggregates it, and writes a daily-summary partition consumed by a BI tool.
processingSteps: 1. A data-availability sensor confirms yesterday's order partition is complete.
2. Airflow triggers the Spark batch job with the run_date parameter.
3. Spark reads only that day's bounded partition and filters to completed orders.
4. It aggregates revenue and order counts by region in parallel across the cluster.
5. It idempotently overwrites yesterday's partition in the daily-summary table, then Airflow triggers the BI refresh.
endToEndExample.output: A `daily_orders` summary partition for the previous day with revenue and order counts per region, ready before the 6 AM SLA.
endToEndExample.monitoring: Airflow tracks DAG run status and SLA; metrics capture job duration, rows in/out, and data-quality checks; alerts fire on failure or SLA breach.
endToEndExample.errorHandling: Transient failures are retried with backoff by the scheduler; because the write is an idempotent partition overwrite, a re-run produces correct data with no duplicates; a failed data-quality check blocks the downstream BI refresh.
endToEndExample.finalResult: Stakeholders reliably get an accurate daily report each morning; the bounded, idempotent, partition-based design makes the pipeline cheap to run off-peak and trivial to backfill if a past day needs correction.

industryUseCases.problem: Computing end-of-day balances, interest accruals, and regulatory reports over enormous transaction volumes.
industryUseCases.solution: Nightly batch jobs (Spark/legacy mainframe) process the full day's transactions to produce balances, statements, and compliance reports.
industryUseCases.benefits: Accurate, auditable end-of-day figures computed cost-effectively over huge volumes with safe reprocessing for corrections.

industryUseCases.problem: Rating and billing billions of call-detail records (CDRs) accumulated throughout the day.
industryUseCases.solution: Scheduled batch pipelines aggregate and rate CDRs to generate daily usage summaries and monthly bills.
industryUseCases.benefits: High-throughput processing of massive record volumes and accurate billing, far cheaper than per-event processing.

industryUseCases.problem: Refreshing data-warehouse tables, dashboards, and ML training datasets from large operational datasets.
industryUseCases.solution: Scheduled ETL/ELT batch jobs (Spark, dbt, scheduled SQL) rebuild summary tables and feature sets nightly or hourly.
industryUseCases.benefits: Reliable, reproducible analytics with simple backfills and cost-efficient off-peak processing.

productionDeepDive.scalability: Partition input by date and scale horizontally by adding executors/nodes. The main scaling challenge is data skew, where uneven key distribution makes a few tasks dominate runtime; mitigate with salting, repartitioning, and adaptive query execution.
productionDeepDive.faultTolerance: Distributed engines recompute lost partitions on worker failure via lineage. Persist source input and design idempotent partition overwrites so a failed job can restart and re-run safely without duplicating output.
productionDeepDive.highAvailability: Run orchestrators (Airflow) in HA mode and use managed/auto-recovering compute (EMR, Dataproc, Databricks). Jobs are restartable, so transient node failures are handled by retries.
productionDeepDive.disasterRecovery: Retain source partitions and store outputs durably; because jobs are idempotent and parameterized by date, the entire history can be rebuilt via backfills after an incident.
productionDeepDive.performanceOptimization: Use columnar formats (Parquet/ORC), partition pruning, predicate pushdown, broadcast joins for small dimensions, and tuned parallelism. Avoid tiny-file problems and address skew to keep tasks balanced.
productionDeepDive.costOptimization: Schedule in off-peak windows, use spot/preemptible instances with retries, auto-scale clusters, and process incrementally (only new partitions) instead of full reloads to minimize compute.
productionDeepDive.securityConsiderations: Encrypt data at rest and in transit, restrict access to input/output stores with least-privilege roles, mask sensitive fields in outputs, and audit job access.
productionDeepDive.monitoringAndObservability: Track job duration trends, SLA adherence, input/output row counts, data-quality results, and resource utilization; alert on failures, SLA breaches, and anomalous runtimes indicating skew or data issues.
productionDeepDive.dataQualityValidation: Run validation gates (row counts, null/key checks, reconciliation against source) after the job; block downstream jobs and alert if checks fail.
productionDeepDive.loggingAndAlerting: Centralize engine and orchestrator logs with run metadata; alert on job failure, SLA breach, data-quality failure, and unusually long runtimes.

recommendedPractices: **Make jobs idempotent:** Overwrite the target partition keyed on the batch window so reruns and backfills are safe.
**Partition by time:** Use date partitions to bound batches, enable pruning, and simplify reprocessing.
**Wait for complete data:** Use sensors/dependencies so jobs run only on complete batches, avoiding partial results.
**Process incrementally:** Run only new/changed partitions instead of full reloads to save cost and time.
engineeringStandards: Every batch job must be parameterized by its batch window (e.g., run/execution date) to support backfills.
Jobs must be idempotent and restartable so retries never duplicate or corrupt data.
Jobs must validate data quality before publishing results to downstream consumers.
designRecommendations: Bound each job to a single, clear time partition for predictable inputs and outputs.
Separate ingestion (landing) from processing so failed processing never requires re-ingestion.
Use columnar storage and partition pruning to minimize I/O.
documentationStandards: Document each job's schedule, upstream dependencies, and SLA.
Document the partition/window key and how to backfill safely.
Record data-quality checks and the action taken on failure.
testingStrategies: Unit-test transformation logic with representative and edge-case data.
Test idempotency by running the same batch twice and asserting identical output.
Test backfills over historical windows and validate row-count reconciliation against source.

commonMistakes.mistake: Writing non-idempotent batch jobs that append without de-duplicating.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Append is the simplest write mode, and engineers don't anticipate reruns or retries.
commonMistakes.impact: Retries and backfills duplicate data, corrupting downstream metrics.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Overwrite the target partition keyed on the batch window (or DELETE-then-INSERT for that window) so reruns are idempotent.

commonMistakes.mistake: Running the job before the batch data has fully landed.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Relying on a fixed clock time instead of confirming data completeness.
commonMistakes.impact: Partial or missing data in outputs that looks valid but is wrong.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Use a data-availability sensor or upstream dependency so the job runs only on a complete batch.

commonMistakes.mistake: Ignoring data skew in distributed batch jobs.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Assuming work is evenly distributed across keys/partitions.
commonMistakes.impact: A few overloaded tasks dominate runtime, blowing the SLA and wasting cluster resources.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Detect skew, and mitigate with salting, repartitioning, broadcast joins, or adaptive query execution.

comparisonSection.optionB: Stream: unbounded data, low latency (sub-second to seconds)
comparisonSection.explanation: Batch processes finite, accumulated datasets on a schedule with results delayed until the run completes. Stream processing handles an unbounded, continuous flow of events and produces results near-instantly per event.

comparisonSection.optionA: Batch: very high throughput, lower freshness
comparisonSection.optionB: Stream: lower per-record overhead amortization, high freshness
comparisonSection.explanation: Batch maximizes throughput and cost-efficiency by amortizing overhead over large groups but data is only as fresh as the last run. Streaming keeps data continuously fresh, ideal for real-time use cases, at higher operational complexity.

comparisonSection.optionA: Batch: simpler logic, mature tooling (Spark, Hadoop, scheduled SQL, Airflow)
comparisonSection.optionB: Stream: more complex (state, windows, exactly-once), tools like Kafka/Flink/Spark Streaming
comparisonSection.explanation: Batch operates on complete datasets, making logic, testing, and reprocessing simpler. Streaming must manage continuous state, event-time windows, late/out-of-order data, and exactly-once semantics, increasing complexity.

beginnerQuestions.question: What is batch processing?
beginnerQuestions.answer: Batch processing collects data over a period into a bounded chunk and processes the whole group together in a single scheduled run, optimizing for high throughput while tolerating higher latency (minutes to hours). Examples include nightly ETL jobs and daily report generation.
beginnerQuestions.explanation: Emphasize bounded data, scheduled execution, and the throughput-over-latency trade-off.

beginnerQuestions.question: What is the difference between batch and stream processing?
beginnerQuestions.answer: Batch processes bounded, finite datasets on a schedule with higher latency and very high throughput. Stream processing handles an unbounded, continuous flow of events with low, near-real-time latency. Batch suits periodic large-volume jobs; streaming suits real-time reactions.
beginnerQuestions.explanation: This is the classic comparison — cover bounded vs. unbounded data, latency, and typical use cases.

intermediateQuestions.question: Why is idempotency important in batch processing, and how do you achieve it?
intermediateQuestions.answer: Idempotency ensures that re-running a job for the same batch produces the same result without duplicating data, which is essential because jobs get retried and backfilled. You achieve it by overwriting the target partition keyed on the batch window (or DELETE-then-INSERT for that window) rather than blindly appending.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: Tie idempotency to safe retries and backfills, and give the partition-overwrite technique.

intermediateQuestions.question: When would you choose batch over streaming?
intermediateQuestions.answer: Choose batch when latency of minutes to hours is acceptable, you process large volumes periodically (daily reports, billing, ETL/ELT loads, ML training data, backfills), and cost-efficiency and simplicity matter more than real-time freshness.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: Frame it as a latency/cost/complexity decision rather than one being universally better.

advancedQuestions.question: How do you handle data skew in a large distributed batch job?
advancedQuestions.answer: Detect skew via the engine's task metrics, then mitigate with key salting (adding a random prefix to spread hot keys), repartitioning to balance task sizes, broadcasting small dimension tables to avoid shuffles, and enabling adaptive query execution which dynamically coalesces and rebalances partitions.
advancedQuestions.explanation: Skew is the top performance problem in distributed batch — name concrete mitigations.

advancedQuestions.question: How do you design a batch pipeline to support safe backfills?
advancedQuestions.answer: Parameterize every job by its batch window (e.g., run date), make writes idempotent via partition overwrite keyed on that window, keep source input partitioned and retained, and ensure jobs have no hidden dependence on 'now'. Then a backfill is simply re-running the job for each historical date, producing correct, non-duplicated data.
advancedQuestions.explanation: Backfills test whether your design is truly window-parameterized and idempotent.

scenarioBasedQuestions.scenario: Your daily batch job sometimes runs twice due to scheduler retries, and stakeholders report duplicated revenue numbers. How do you fix it?
scenarioBasedQuestions.thinkingProcess: Duplicates on rerun point to a non-idempotent write (append) rather than a partition-scoped overwrite. The fix is to make the write idempotent so reruns replace rather than add data for that window.
scenarioBasedQuestions.expectedAnswer: Make the job idempotent: change the write to overwrite only the run-date partition (or DELETE-then-INSERT for that date) keyed on the batch window, so a rerun replaces that day's data instead of appending. Verify by running the same batch twice and asserting identical output.

systemDesignQuestions.problemStatement: Design a batch pipeline to produce hourly aggregated metrics from high-volume web event logs with a 15-minute post-hour SLA.
systemDesignQuestions.designApproach: Land events in hourly date/hour partitions in object storage. Use an Airflow sensor to detect a complete hour partition, then trigger a Spark job parameterized by the hour that aggregates that bounded partition and idempotently overwrites the corresponding output partition. Validate counts, then publish.
systemDesignQuestions.tradeOffs: Batch (even hourly) is simpler and cheaper than streaming and meets a 15-minute SLA, but it cannot give sub-second freshness. Smaller windows increase scheduling overhead and small-file risk; larger windows increase latency.
systemDesignQuestions.scalingStrategy: Partition by hour for pruning, scale Spark executors with volume, mitigate skew, use columnar formats, and process only new partitions. If freshness needs tighten to seconds, migrate hot metrics to streaming/micro-batch.

cheatSheet.oneLineDefinition: Batch processing runs jobs over bounded chunks of accumulated data on a schedule, optimizing for high throughput while tolerating minutes-to-hours latency.
keyConcepts: Bounded data processed in groups, not per-event.
Idempotency via partition overwrite enables safe reruns/backfills.
Windows/partitions (usually by date) define the batch unit.
Tools: Spark, Hadoop MapReduce, scheduled SQL; orchestrated by Airflow/cron.
formulas: N/A — batch processing is a design pattern with no governing formula (throughput vs. latency is a qualitative trade-off).
commands: spark-submit job.py 2026-06-17  # run batch for a bounded date
Airflow: sensor -> SparkSubmitOperator/SQL operator on a schedule with retries
interviewPoints: Batch = bounded data, scheduled, high throughput, higher latency.
Contrast with stream: unbounded data, low latency, more complex.
Idempotency (partition overwrite) is essential for retries/backfills.
Skew is the main distributed-batch performance problem.
Batch and stream are complementary (Lambda/Kappa), not replacements.
quickNotes: Wait for complete data with sensors before running.
Parameterize by batch window to support backfills.
Run off-peak on spot instances to cut cost.
Micro-batch bridges batch and streaming for near-real-time needs.

keyTakeaways: Batch processing handles bounded chunks of accumulated data together on a schedule, trading higher latency for very high throughput and cost-efficiency.
Core concepts are bounded datasets, scheduled/triggered jobs, time-based windows/partitions, and idempotency for safe reruns and backfills.
It is implemented with engines like Spark and Hadoop MapReduce and scheduled SQL, orchestrated by tools such as Airflow.
The classic contrast with stream processing is bounded vs. unbounded data and high-latency/high-throughput vs. low-latency/real-time; the two are complementary, not competitors.
Production batch design relies on partitioning by time, idempotent partition overwrites, waiting for complete data, mitigating skew, and running cost-effectively off-peak.
